name: What Does a New Home Build Really Involve?

step.name: Step 1: Land Acquisition and Site Preparation. Before anything can be built, you need the right piece of land. This involves surveying, soil testing, and sometimes clearing the site. It's crucial to understand zoning regulations and potential environmental factors before purchasing. This phase can take several months, including due diligence and closing on the property.
step.text: Step 1: Land Acquisition and Site Preparation. Before anything can be built, you need the right piece of land. This involves surveying, soil testing, and sometimes clearing the site. It's crucial to understand zoning regulations and potential environmental factors before purchasing. This phase can take several months, including due diligence and closing on the property.

step.name: Step 2: Design and Engineering. This is where your vision takes shape. You'll work with architects and engineers to create detailed blueprints, including structural, mechanical, electrical, and plumbing plans. This phase also involves selecting finishes and materials. Expect this to take 3-6 months, depending on the complexity of the design and revisions.

step.name: Step 3: Permitting and Approvals. Once designs are finalized, your contractor will submit them to the local building department for permits. This is a critical bureaucratic step that ensures your home meets all local codes and safety standards. Permit approval times vary widely by jurisdiction, from a few weeks to several months.
step.text: Step 3: Permitting and Approvals. Once designs are finalized, your contractor will submit them to the local building department for permits. This is a critical bureaucratic step that ensures your home meets all local codes and safety standards. Permit approval times vary widely by jurisdiction, from a few weeks to several months.

step.name: Step 4: Foundation and Framing. With permits in hand, construction begins. The foundation is poured, followed by the framing, which forms the skeleton of your home. This includes walls, floors, and roof structures. Inspections are typically required after each major phase. This stage can take 1-3 months, depending on the size and complexity of the home.
step.text: Step 4: Foundation and Framing. With permits in hand, construction begins. The foundation is poured, followed by the framing, which forms the skeleton of your home. This includes walls, floors, and roof structures. Inspections are typically required after each major phase. This stage can take 1-3 months, depending on the size and complexity of the home.

step.name: Step 5: Rough-Ins (Electrical, Plumbing, HVAC). After framing, the rough-ins for all utilities are installed. This means running wires, pipes, and ductwork through the walls, ceilings, and floors before they are closed up. Again, inspections are vital here. This phase generally takes 4-8 weeks.
step.text: Step 5: Rough-Ins (Electrical, Plumbing, HVAC). After framing, the rough-ins for all utilities are installed. This means running wires, pipes, and ductwork through the walls, ceilings, and floors before they are closed up. Again, inspections are vital here. This phase generally takes 4-8 weeks.

step.name: Step 6: Exterior Work and Insulation. Once rough-ins are complete, the exterior envelope of the home is finished, including roofing, siding, windows, and doors. Insulation is also installed to improve energy efficiency. This can take 2-3 months.
step.text: Step 6: Exterior Work and Insulation. Once rough-ins are complete, the exterior envelope of the home is finished, including roofing, siding, windows, and doors. Insulation is also installed to improve energy efficiency. This can take 2-3 months.

step.name: Step 7: Interior Finishes. This is where your home really starts to look like a home. Drywall is hung and finished, followed by painting, flooring, cabinetry, countertops, and light fixtures. This is often the longest phase, spanning 2-4 months.

step.name: Step 8: Final Touches and Landscaping. The last steps involve installing appliances, final electrical and plumbing fixtures, and completing any landscaping. A final walk-through with your contractor ensures everything is perfect. This final stage usually takes 2-4 weeks, leading to your occupancy permit.
